entries.5c75e6db5dc69e9bdcfc79e63ec1e0bdfd199e39: <div sID="gen18952" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="28" osisID="Ezek.28" sID="Ezek.28"/> <div eID="gen18952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18953" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18954" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. A prediction of the fall and ruin of the king of Tyre, who, in the destruction of that city, is particularly set up as a mark for God's arrows, <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.1-Ezek.28.10">ver. 1-10</reference>. II. A lamentation for the king of Tyre, when he has thus fallen, though he falls by his own iniquity, <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.11-Ezek.28.19">ver. 11-19</reference>. III. A prophecy of the destruction of Zidon, which as in the neighbourhood of Tyre and had a dependence upon it, <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.20-Ezek.28.23">ver. 20-23</reference>. IV. A promise of the restoration of the Israel of God, though in the day of their calamity they were insulted over by their neighbours, <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.24-Ezek.28.26">ver. 24-26</reference>.
entries.6c16e270f209f32b2b0894013a635532891bd419: <div eID="gen18954" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18953" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Fall of the Prince of Tyre. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18955" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came again unto me, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Son of man, say unto the prince of Tyrus, Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Because thine heart <hi type="italic">is</hi> lifted up, and thou hast said, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> a God, I sit <hi type="italic">in</hi> the seat of God, in the midst of the seas; yet thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> a man, and not God, though thou set thine heart as the heart of God: <hi type="super">3</hi> Behold, thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> wiser than Daniel; there is no secret that they can hide from thee: <hi type="super">4</hi> With thy wisdom and with thine understanding thou hast gotten thee riches, and hast gotten gold and silver into thy treasures: <hi type="super">5</hi> By thy great wisdom <hi type="italic">and</hi> by thy traffick hast thou increased thy riches, and thine heart is lifted up because of thy riches: <hi type="super">6</hi> Therefore thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Because thou hast set thine heart as the heart of God; <hi type="super">7</hi> Behold, therefore I will bring strangers upon thee, the terrible of the nations: and they shall draw their swords against the beauty of thy wisdom, and they shall defile thy brightness. <hi type="super">8</hi> They shall bring thee down to the pit, and thou shalt die the deaths of <hi type="italic">them that are</hi> slain in the midst of the seas. <hi type="super">9</hi> Wilt thou yet say before him that slayeth thee, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> God? but thou <hi type="italic">shalt be</hi> a man, and no God, in the hand of him that slayeth thee. <hi type="super">10</hi> Thou shalt die the deaths of the uncircumcised by the hand of strangers: for I have spoken <hi type="italic">it,</hi> saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <div eID="gen18955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18956" type="x-p"/> We had done with Tyrus in the foregoing chapter, but now the prince of Tyrus is to be singled out from the rest. Here is something to be said to him by himself, a <hi type="italic">message to him from God,</hi> which the prophet must send him, whether he will hear or whether he will forbear. <div eID="gen18956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18957" type="x-p"/> I. He must tell him of his pride. His people are proud (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.3">ch. xxvii. 3</reference>) and so is he; and they shall both be made to know that <hi type="italic">God resists the proud.</hi> Let us see, 1. What were the expressions of his pride: <hi type="italic">His heart was lifted up,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.2">v. 2</reference>. He had a great conceit of himself, was puffed up with an opinion of his own sufficiency, and looked with disdain upon all about him. Out of the abundance of the pride of his heart he said, <hi type="italic">I am a god;</hi> he did not only say it in his heart, but had the impudence to speak it out. God has said of princes, <hi type="italic">They are gods</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.82.6">Ps. lxxxii. 6</reference>); but it does not become them to say so of themselves; it is a high affront to him who is <hi type="italic">God alone,</hi> and will not give his glory to another. He thought that the city of Tyre had as necessary a dependence upon him as the world has upon the God that made it, and that he was himself independent as God and unaccountable to any. He thought himself to have as much wisdom and strength as God himself, and as incontestable an authority, and that his prerogatives were as absolute and his word as much a law as the word of God. He challenged divine honours, and expected to be praised and admired as a god, and doubted not to be deified, among other heroes, after his death as a great benefactor to the world. Thus the king of Babylon said, <hi type="italic">I will be like the Most High</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.14">Isa. xiv. 14</reference>), not like the <hi type="italic">Most Holy. "I am the strong God,</hi> and therefore will not be contradicted, because I cannot be controlled. <hi type="italic">I sit in the seat of God;</hi> I sit <hi type="italic">as high</hi> as God, my throne equal with his. <hi type="italic">Divisum imperium cum Jove Cæsar habet—Cæsar divides dominion with Jove.</hi> I sit as safely as God, as safely <hi type="italic">in the heart of the seas,</hi> and as far out of the reach of danger, as he in the <hi type="italic">height of heaven.</hi>" He thinks his guards of men of war about his throne as pompous and potent as the hosts of angels that are about the throne of God. He is put in mind of his meanness and mortality, and, since he needs to be told, he shall be told, that self-evident truth, <hi type="italic">Thou art a man, and not God,</hi> a depending creature; thou art <hi type="italic">flesh, and not spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.31.3">Isa. xxxi. 3</reference>. Note, Men must be made to know that they are <hi type="italic">but men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.9.20">Ps. ix. 20</reference>. The greatest wits, the greatest potentates, the greatest saints, are <hi type="italic">men, and not gods.</hi> Jesus Christ was both God and man. The king of Tyre, though he has such a mighty influence upon all about him, and with the help of his riches bears a mighty sway, though he has tribute and presents brought to his court with as much devotion as if they were sacrifices to his altar, though he is flattered by his courtiers and made a god of by his poets, yet, after all, he is <hi type="italic">but a man;</hi> he knows it; he fears it. But <hi type="italic">he sets his heart as the heart of God;</hi> "Thou hast conceited thyself to be a god, hast compared thyself with God, thinking thyself as wise and strong, and as fit to govern the world, as he." It was the ruin of our first parents, and ours in them, that they would be <hi type="italic">as gods,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.3.5">Gen. iii. 5</reference>. And still that corrupt nature which inclines men to set up themselves as their own masters, to do what they will, and their own carvers, to have what they will, their own end, to live to themselves, and their own felicity, to enjoy themselves, <hi type="italic">sets their hearts as the heart of God,</hi> invades his prerogatives, and catches at the flowers of his crown—a presumption that cannot go unpunished. <div eID="gen18957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18958" type="x-p"/> 2. We are here told what it was that he was proud of. (1.) His wisdom. It is probable that this prince of Tyre was a man of very good natural parts, a philosopher, and well read in all the parts of learning that were then in vogue, at least a politician, and one that had great dexterity in managing the affairs of state. And then he thought himself <hi type="italic">wiser than Daniel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.3">v. 3</reference>. We found, before, that Daniel, though now but a young man, was celebrated for his prevalency in prayer, <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.14">ch. xiv. 14</reference>. Here we find he was famous for his prudence in the management of the affairs of this world, a great scholar and statesman, and withal a great saint, and yet not a prince, but a poor captive. It was strange that under such external disadvantages his lustre should shine forth, so that he had become <hi type="italic">wise to a proverb.</hi> When the king of Tyre dreams himself to be a god he says, I am <hi type="italic">wiser than Daniel. There is no secret that they can hide from thee.</hi> Probably he challenged all about him to <hi type="italic">prove him with questions,</hi> as Solomon was proved, and he had unriddled all their enigmas, had solved all their problems, and none of them all could puzzle him. He had perhaps been successful in discovering plots, and diving into the counsels of the neighbouring princes, and therefore thought himself omniscient, and that no thought could be withholden from him; therefore he said, <hi type="italic">I am a god.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">Knowledge puffeth up;</hi> it is hard to know much and not to know it too well and to be elevated with it. He that was <hi type="italic">wiser than Daniel</hi> was prouder than Lucifer. Those therefore that are knowing must study to be humble and to evidence that they are so. (2.) His wealth. That way his wisdom led him; it is not said that by his wisdom he searched into the arcana either of nature or government, modelled the state better than it was, or made better laws, or advanced the interests of the commonwealth of learning; but his <hi type="italic">wisdom and understanding</hi> were of use to him in <hi type="italic">traffic.</hi> As some of the kings of Judah <hi type="italic">loved husbandry</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.26.10">2 Chron. xxvi. 10</reference>), so the king of Tyre loved merchandise, and by it he <hi type="italic">got riches, increased his riches, and filled his treasures with gold and silver,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.4-Ezek.28.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. See what the wisdom of this world is; those are cried up as the wisest men that know how to get money and by right or wrong to raise estates; and yet really <hi type="italic">this their way is their folly,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.49.13">Ps. xlix. 13</reference>. It was the folly of the king of Tyre, [1.] That he attributed the increase of his wealth to himself and not to the providence of God, forgetting him who <hi type="italic">gave him power to get wealth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.8.17-Deut.8.18">Deut. viii. 17, 18</reference>. [2.] That he thought himself a wise man because he was a rich man; whereas a fool may have an estate (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.19">Eccl. ii. 19</reference>), yea, and a fool may get an estate, for the world has been often observed to favour such, <hi type="italic">when bread is not to the wise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.11">Eccl. ix. 11</reference>. [3.] That <hi type="italic">his heart was lifted up because of his riches,</hi> because of the increase of his wealth, which made him so haughty and secure, so insolent and imperious, and which <hi type="italic">set his heart as the heart of God.</hi> The <hi type="italic">man of sin,</hi> when he had a great deal of worldly pomp and power, <hi type="italic">showed himself as a god,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.4">2 Thess. ii. 4</reference>. Those who are rich in this world have therefore need to charge that upon themselves which the word of God charges upon them, <hi type="italic">that they be not high-minded,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.17">1 Tim. vi. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen18958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18959" type="x-p"/> II. Since <hi type="italic">pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall,</hi> he must bell him of that destruction, of that fall, which was now hastening on as the just punishment of his presumption in setting up himself a rival with God. "Because thou hast pretended to be a god (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.6">v. 6</reference>), therefore thou shalt not be long a man," <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.7">v. 7</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen18959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18960" type="x-p"/> 1. The instruments of his destruction: <hi type="italic">I will bring strangers upon thee</hi>—the Chaldeans, whom we do not find mentioned among the many nations and countries that traded with Tyre, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.1-Ezek.27.36">ch. xxvii.</reference> If any of those nations had been brought against it, they would have had some compassion upon it, for old acquaintance-sake; but these strangers will have none. They are people of a <hi type="italic">strange language,</hi> which the king of Tyre himself, wise as he is, perhaps understands not. They are the <hi type="italic">terrible of the nations;</hi> it was an army made up of many nations, and it was at this time the most formidable both for strength and fury. These God has at command, and these he will bring upon the king of Tyre. <div eID="gen18960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18961" type="x-p"/> 2. The extremity of the destruction: <hi type="italic">They shall draw their swords against the beauty of thy wisdom</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.7">v. 7</reference>), against all those things which thou gloriest in as thy beauty and the production of thy wisdom. Note, It is just with God that our enemies should make that their prey which we have made our pride. The king of Tyre's palace, his treasury, his city, his navy, his army, these he glories in as his brightness, these, he thinks, made him illustrious and glorious as a god on earth. But all these the victorious enemy shall defile, shall deface, shall deform. He thought them sacred, things that none durst touch; but the conquerors shall seize them as common things, and spoil the brightness of them. But, whatever becomes of what he has, surely his person is sacred. No (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall bring thee down to the pit,</hi> to the grave; thou shalt <hi type="italic">die the death.</hi> And, (1.) It shall not be an honourable death, but an ignominious one. He shall be so vilified in his death that he may despair of being deified after his death. He shall die <hi type="italic">the deaths of those that are slain in the midst of the seas,</hi> that have no honour done them at their death, but their dead bodies are immediately thrown overboard, without any ceremony or mark of distinction, to be a feast for the fish. Tyre is <hi type="italic">likely to be destroyed in the midst of the sea</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.32">ch. xxvii. 32</reference>) and the prince of Tyre shall fare no better than the people. (2.) It shall not be a happy death, but a miserable one. He shall <hi type="italic">die the deaths of the uncircumcised</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.10">v. 10</reference>), of those that are strangers to God and not in covenant with him, and therefore die under his wrath and curse. It is <hi type="italic">deaths,</hi> a double death, temporal and eternal, the death both of body and soul. He shall die the <hi type="italic">second death;</hi> that is dying miserably indeed. The sentence of death here passed upon the king of Tyre is ratified by a divine authority: <hi type="italic">I have spoken it, saith the Lord God.</hi> And what he has said he will do. None can gainsay it, nor will he unsay it. <div eID="gen18961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18962" type="x-p"/> 3. The effectual disproof that this will be of all his pretensions to deity (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.9">v. 9</reference>): "When the conqueror sets his sword to thy breast, and thou seest no way of escape, <hi type="italic">wilt thou then say, I am God?</hi> Wilt thou then have such a conceit of thyself as thou now hast? No; thy being overpowered by death, and by the fear of it, will force thee to own that thou art not a god, but a weak, timorous, trembling, dying man. <hi type="italic">In the hand of him that slays thee</hi> (in the hand of God, and of the instruments that he employed) <hi type="italic">thou shalt be a man, and not God,</hi> utterly unable to resist, and help thyself." <hi type="italic">I have said, You are gods; but you shall die like men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.82.6-Ps.82.7">Ps. lxxxii. 6, 7</reference>. Note, Those who pretend to be rivals with God shall be forced one way or other to let fall their claims. Death at furthest, when we come into his hand, will make us know that we are men.
entries.6bf4bd5bb0aa2e67b535ed701ab4b3138019b79b: <div eID="gen18962" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Fall of the Prince of Tyre. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18963" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Moreover the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">12</hi> Son of man, take up a lamentation upon the king of Tyrus, and say unto him, Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Thou sealest up the sum, full of wisdom, and perfect in beauty. <hi type="super">13</hi> Thou hast been in Eden the garden of God; every precious stone <hi type="italic">was</hi> thy covering, the sardius, topaz, and the diamond, the beryl, the onyx, and the jasper, the sapphire, the emerald, and the carbuncle, and gold: the workmanship of thy tabrets and of thy pipes was prepared in thee in the day that thou wast created. <hi type="super">14</hi> Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> the anointed cherub that covereth; and I have set thee <hi type="italic">so:</hi> thou wast upon the holy mountain of God; thou hast walked up and down in the midst of the stones of fire. <hi type="super">15</hi> Thou <hi type="italic">wast</hi> perfect in thy ways from the day that thou wast created, till iniquity was found in thee. <hi type="super">16</hi> By the multitude of thy merchandise they have filled the midst of thee with violence, and thou hast sinned: therefore I will cast thee as profane out of the mountain of God: and I will destroy thee, O covering cherub, from the midst of the stones of fire. <hi type="super">17</hi> Thine heart was lifted up because of thy beauty, thou hast corrupted thy wisdom by reason of thy brightness: I will cast thee to the ground, I will lay thee before kings, that they may behold thee. <hi type="super">18</hi> Thou hast defiled thy sanctuaries by the multitude of thine iniquities, by the iniquity of thy traffick; therefore will I bring forth a fire from the midst of thee, it shall devour thee, and I will bring thee to ashes upon the earth in the sight of all them that behold thee. <hi type="super">19</hi> All they that know thee among the people shall be astonished at thee: thou shalt be a terror, and never <hi type="italic">shalt</hi> thou <hi type="italic">be</hi> any more. <div eID="gen18963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18964" type="x-p"/> As after the prediction of the ruin of Tyre (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.1-Ezek.26.21">ch. xxvi.</reference>) followed a pathetic lamentation for it (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.1-Ezek.27.36">ch. xxvii.</reference>), so after the ruin of the king of Tyre is foretold it is bewailed. <div eID="gen18964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18965" type="x-p"/> I. This is commonly understood of the prince who then reigned over Tyre, spoken to, <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.2">v. 2</reference>. His name was <hi type="italic">Ethbaal,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Ithobalus,</hi> as Diodorus Siculus calls him that was king of Tyre when Nebuchadnezzar destroyed it. He was, it seems, upon all external accounts an accomplished man, very great and famous; but his iniquity was his ruin. Many expositors have suggested that besides the literal sense of this lamentation there is an allegory in it, and that it is an allusion to the fall of the angels that sinned, who undid themselves by their pride. And (as is usual in texts that have a mystical meaning) some passages here refer primarily to the king of Tyre, as that of his merchandises, others to the angels, as that of being <hi type="italic">in the holy mountain of God.</hi> But, if there be any thing mystical in it (as perhaps there may), I shall rather refer it to the fall of Adam, which seems to be glanced at, <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.13">v. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thou hast been in Eden the garden of God, and that in the day thou wast created.</hi> <div eID="gen18965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18966" type="x-p"/> II. Some think that by <hi type="italic">the king of Tyre</hi> is meant the whole royal family, this including also the foregoing kings, and looking as far back as Hiram, king of Tyre. The then governor is called <hi type="italic">prince</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.2">v. 2</reference>); but he that is here lamented is called <hi type="italic">king.</hi> The court of Tyre with its kings had for many ages been famous; but sin ruins it. Now we may observe two things here:— <div eID="gen18966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18967" type="x-p"/> 1. What was the renown of the king of Tyre. He is here spoken of as having lived in great splendour, <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.12-Ezek.28.15">v. 12-15</reference>. He as a man, but it is here owned that he was a very considerable man and one that made a mighty figure in his day. (1.) He far exceeded other men. Hiram and other kings of Tyre had done so in their time; and the reigning king perhaps had not come short of any of them: <hi type="italic">Thou sealest up the sum full of wisdom and perfect in beauty.</hi> But the powers of human nature and the prosperity of human life seemed in him to be at the highest pitch. He was looked upon to be as wise as the reason of men could make him, and as happy as the wealth of this world and the enjoyment of it could make him; in him you might see the utmost that both could do; and therefore <hi type="italic">seal up the sum,</hi> for nothing can be added; he is a complete man, perfect <hi type="italic">in suo genere—in his kind.</hi> (2.) He seemed to be as wise and happy as Adam in innocency (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.13">v. 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou hast been in Eden,</hi> even <hi type="italic">in the garden of God;</hi> thou hast lived as it were in paradise all thy days, hast had a full enjoyment of every thing that is <hi type="italic">good for food</hi> or <hi type="italic">pleasant to the eyes,</hi> and an uncontroverted dominion over all about thee, as Adam had." One instance of the magnificence of the king of Tyre is, that he outdid all others princes in jewels, which those have the greatest plenty of that trade most abroad, as he did: <hi type="italic">Every precious stone</hi> was <hi type="italic">his covering.</hi> There is a great variety of precious stones; but he had of every sort and in such plenty that besides what were treasured up in his cabinet, and were the ornaments of his crown, he had his clothes trimmed with them; they were his <hi type="italic">covering.</hi> Nay (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.14">v. 14</reference>), he <hi type="italic">walked up and down in the midst of the stones of fire,</hi> that is, these precious stones, which glittered and sparkled like fire. His rooms were in a manner set round with jewels, so that he walked in the midst of them, and then fancied himself as glorious as if, like God, he had been surrounded by so many angels, who are compared to a <hi type="italic">flame of fire.</hi> And, if he be such an admirer of precious stones as to think them as bright as angels, no wonder that he is such an admirer of himself as to think himself as great as God. Nine several sorts of previous stones are here named, which were all in the high priest's ephod. Perhaps they are particularly named because he, in his pride, used to speak particularly of them, and tell those about him, with a great deal of foolish pleasure, "This is such a precious stone, of such a value, and so and so are its virtues." Thus is he upbraided with his vanity. <hi type="italic">Gold</hi> is mentioned last, as far inferior in value to those precious stones; and he used to speak of it accordingly. Another thing that made him think his palace a paradise was the curious music he had, the <hi type="italic">tabrets and pipes,</hi> hand-instruments and wind-instruments. The <hi type="italic">workmanship</hi> of these was extraordinary, and they were prepared for him on purpose; prepared <hi type="italic">in thee,</hi> the pronoun is feminine—<hi type="italic">in thee,</hi> O Tyre! or it denotes that the king was effeminate in doting on such things. They were prepared <hi type="italic">in the day he was created,</hi> that is, either born, or created king; they were made on purpose to celebrate the joys either of his birth-day or of his coronation-day. These he prided himself much in, and would have all that came to see his palace take notice of them. (3.) He looked like an incarnate angel (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou art the anointed cherub that covers</hi> or <hi type="italic">protects;</hi> that is, he looked upon himself as a guardian angel to his people, so bright, so strong, so faithful, appointed to this office and qualified for it. Anointed kings should be to their subjects as anointed cherubim, that cover them with the wings of their power; and, when they are such, God will own them. Their advancement was from him: <hi type="italic">I have set thee so.</hi> Some think, because mention was made of Eden, that it refers to the cherub set on the east of Eden to cover it, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.24">Gen. iii. 24</reference>. He thought himself as able to guard his city from all invaders as that angel was for his charge. Or it may refer to the cherubim in the most holy place, whose wings covered the ark; he thought himself as bright as one of them. (4.) He appeared in as much splendour as the high priest when he was clothed with his garments for glory and beauty: "<hi type="italic">Thou wast upon the holy mountain of God,</hi> as president of the temple built on that holy mountain; thou didst look as great, and with as much majesty and authority, as ever the high priest did when he walked in the temple, which was <hi type="italic">garnished with precious stones</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.3.6">2 Chron. iii. 6</reference>), and had his habit on, which had precious stones both in the breast and on the shoulders; in that he seemed to <hi type="italic">walk in the midst of the stones of fire.</hi>" Thus glorious is the king of Tyre; at least he thinks himself so. <div eID="gen18967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18968" type="x-p"/> 2. Let us now see what was the ruin of the king of Tyre, what it was that stained his glory and laid all this honour in the dust (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.15">v. 15</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou wast perfect in thy ways;</hi> thou didst prosper in all thy affairs and every thing went well with thee; thou hadst not only a clear, but a bright reputation, <hi type="italic">from the day thou wast created,</hi> the day of thy accession to the throne, <hi type="italic">till iniquity was found in thee;</hi> and that spoiled all." This may perhaps allude to the deplorable case of the angels that fell, and of our first parents, both of whom <hi type="italic">were perfect in their ways till iniquity was found in them.</hi> And when iniquity was once <hi type="italic">found in him</hi> it increased; he grew worse and worse, as appears (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.18">v. 18</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou hast defiled thy sanctuaries;</hi> thou hast lost the benefit of all that which thou thoughtest sacred, and in which, as in a sanctuary, thou thoughtest to take refuge; these thou hast <hi type="italic">defiled,</hi> and so exposed thyself <hi type="italic">by the multitude of thy iniquities.</hi>" Now observe, <div eID="gen18968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18969" type="x-p"/> (1.) What the iniquity was that was the ruin of the king of Tyre. [1.] The <hi type="italic">iniquity of his traffic</hi> (so it is called, <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.18">v. 18</reference>), both his and his people's, for their sin is charged upon him, because he connived at it and set them a bad example (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">By the multitude of thy merchandise they have filled the midst of thee with violence,</hi> and thus <hi type="italic">thou hast sinned.</hi> The king had so much to do with his merchandise, and was so wholly intent upon the gains of that, that he took no care to do justice, to give redress to those that suffered wrong and to protect them from violence; nay, in the multiplicity of business, wrong was done to many by oversight; and in his dealings he made use of his power to invade the rights of those he dealt with. Note, Those that have much to do in the world are in great danger of doing much amiss; and it is hard to deal with many without violence to some. Trades are called mysteries; but too many make them mysteries of iniquity. [2.] His pride and vain-glory (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.17">v. 17</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thy heart was lifted up because of thy beauty;</hi> thou wast in love with thyself, and thy own shadow. And thus <hi type="italic">thou hast corrupted thy wisdom by reason of the brightness,</hi> the pomp and splendour, wherein thou livedst." He gazed so much upon this that it dazzled his eyes and prevented him from seeing his way. He appeared so puffed up with his greatness that it bereaved him both of his wisdom and of the reputation of it. He really became a <hi type="italic">fool in glorying.</hi> Those make a bad bargain for themselves that part with their wisdom for the gratifying of their gaiety, and, to please a vain humour, lose a real excellency. <div eID="gen18969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18970" type="x-p"/> (2.) What the ruin was that this iniquity brought him to. [1.] He was thrown out of his dignity and dislodged from his palace, which he took to be his paradise and temple (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will cast thee as profane out of the mountain of God.</hi> His kingly power was high as a <hi type="italic">mountain,</hi> setting him above others; it was a <hi type="italic">mountain of God,</hi> for the powers that be are ordained of God, and have something in them that is sacred; but, having abused his power, he is reckoned profane, and is therefore deposed and expelled. He disgraces the crown he wears, and so has forfeited it, and shall be destroyed <hi type="italic">from the midst of the stones of fire,</hi> the precious stones with which his palace was garnished, as the temple was; and they shall be no protection to him. [2.] He was exposed to contempt and disgrace, and trampled upon by his neighbours: "<hi type="italic">I will cast thee to the ground</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.17">v. 17</reference>), will cast thee among the <hi type="italic">pavement-stones,</hi> from the midst of the <hi type="italic">precious stones,</hi> and will <hi type="italic">lay thee</hi> a rueful spectacle <hi type="italic">before kings, that they may behold thee</hi> and take warning by thee not to be proud and oppressive." [3.] He was quite consumed, his city and he in it: <hi type="italic">I will bring forth a fire from the midst of thee.</hi> The conquerors, when they have plundered the city, will kindle a fire in the heart of it, which shall lay it, and the palace particularly, in ashes. Or it may be taken more generally for the fire of God's judgments, which shall devour both prince and people, and bring all the glory of both <hi type="italic">to ashes upon the earth;</hi> and this fire shall be <hi type="italic">brought forth from the midst of thee.</hi> All God's judgments upon sinners take rise from themselves; they are devoured by a fire of their own kindling. [4.] He was hereby made a terrible example of divine vengeance. Thus he is reduced <hi type="italic">in the sight of all those that behold him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">Those that know him shall be astonished at him,</hi> and shall wonder how one that stood so high could be brought so low. The king of Tyre's palace, like the temple at Jerusalem, when it is destroyed shall be <hi type="italic">an astonishment and a hissing,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.20-2Chr.7.21">2 Chron. vii. 20, 21</reference>. So fell the king of Tyre.
entries.46cd029fb9488a00a88508978ae54990bc7f09d6: <div eID="gen18970" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Fall of Zidon. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18971" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> Again the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">21</hi> Son of man, set thy face against Zidon, and prophesy against it, <hi type="super">22</hi> And say, Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Behold, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> against thee, O Zidon; and I will be glorified in the midst of thee: and they shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , when I shall have executed judgments in her, and shall be sanctified in her. <hi type="super">23</hi> For I will send into her pestilence, and blood into her streets; and the wounded shall be judged in the midst of her by the sword upon her on every side; and they shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">24</hi> And there shall be no more a pricking brier unto the house of Israel, nor <hi type="italic">any</hi> grieving thorn of all <hi type="italic">that are</hi> round about them, that despised them; and they shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <hi type="super">25</hi> Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; When I shall have gathered the house of Israel from the people among whom they are scattered, and shall be sanctified in them in the sight of the heathen, then shall they dwell in their land that I have given to my servant Jacob. <hi type="super">26</hi> And they shall dwell safely therein, and shall build houses, and plant vineyards; yea, they shall dwell with confidence, when I have executed judgments upon all those that despise them round about them; and they shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> their God. <div eID="gen18971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18972" type="x-p"/> God's glory is his great end, both in all the good and in all the evil which <hi type="italic">proceed out of the mouth of the Most High;</hi> so we find in these verses. 1. God will be glorified in the destruction of Zidon, a city that lay near to Tyre, was more ancient, but not so considerable, had a dependence upon it and stood and fell with it. God says here, <hi type="italic">I am against thee, O Zidon! and I will be glorified in the midst of thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.22">v. 22</reference>. And again, "Those that would not know by gentler methods shall be made to <hi type="italic">know that I am the Lord,</hi> and I alone, and that I am a just and jealous God, <hi type="italic">when I shall have executed judgments in her,</hi> destroying judgments, when I shall have done execution according to justice and according to the sentence passed, and so shall be <hi type="italic">sanctified in her.</hi>" The Zidonians, it should seem, were more addicted to idolatry than the Tyrians were, who, being men of business and large conversation, were less under the power of bigotry and superstition. The Zidonians were noted for the worship of Ashtaroth; Solomon introduced it, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.5">1 Kings xi. 5</reference>. Jezebel was daughter to the king of Zidon, who brought the worship of Baal into Israel (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.31">1 Kings xvi. 31</reference>); so that God had been much dishonoured by the Zidonians. Now, says he, <hi type="italic">I will be glorified, I will be sanctified.</hi> The Zidonians were borderers upon the land of Israel, where God was known, and where they might have got the knowledge of him and have learned to glorify him; but, instead of that, they seduced Israel to the worship of their idols. Note, When God is sanctified he is glorified, for his holiness is his glory; and those whom he is not sanctified and glorified by he will be sanctified and glorified upon, by executing judgments upon them, which declare him a just avenger of his own and his people's injured honour. The judgments that shall be executed upon Zidon are war and pestilence, two wasting depopulating judgments, <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.23">v. 23</reference>. They are God's messengers, which he sends on his errands, and they shall accomplish that for which he sends them. <hi type="italic">Pestilence</hi> and <hi type="italic">blood</hi> shall be sent <hi type="italic">into her streets;</hi> there the dead bodies of those shall lie who perished, some by the plague, occasioned perhaps through ill diet when the city was besieged, and some by the sword of the enemy, most likely the Chaldean armies, when the city was taken, and all were put to the sword. Thus the wounded shall be judged; when they are dying of their wounds they shall judge themselves, and others shall say, They justly fall. Or, as some read it, <hi type="italic">They shall be punished by the sword,</hi> that sword which has commission to destroy <hi type="italic">on every side.</hi> It is God that judges, and he will overcome. Nor is it Tyre and Zidon only on which God would execute judgments, but on all those that despised his people Israel, and triumphed in their calamities; for this was now God's controversy with the nations that were <hi type="italic">round about them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.26">v. 26</reference>. Note, When God's people are under his correcting hand for their faults he takes care, as he did concerning malefactors that were scourged, <hi type="italic">that they shall not seem vile</hi> to those that are about them, and therefore takes it ill of those who despise them and so <hi type="italic">help forward the affliction</hi> when he is but <hi type="italic">a little displeased,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.1.15">Zech. i. 15</reference>. God regards them even in their low estate; and therefore let not men despise them. 2. God will be glorified in the restoration of his people to their former safety and prosperity. God had been dishonoured by the sins of his people, and their sufferings too had given occasion to the enemy to blaspheme (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.5">Isa. lii. 5</reference>); but God will now both cure them of their sins and ease them of their troubles, and so <hi type="italic">will be sanctified in them in the sight of the heathen,</hi> will recover the honour of his holiness, to the satisfaction of all the world, <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.25">v. 25</reference>. For, (1.) They shall return to the possession of their own land again: <hi type="italic">I will gather the house of Israel</hi> out of their dispersions, in answer to that prayer (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.27">Ps. cvi. 27</reference>), <hi type="italic">Save us, O Lord our God! and gather us from among the heathen;</hi> and in pursuance of that promise (<reference osisRef="Deut.30.4">Deut. xxx. 4</reference>), Thence will <hi type="italic">the Lord thy God gather thee.</hi> Being gathered, they shall be brought in a body, to <hi type="italic">dwell in the land that I have given to my servant Jacob.</hi> God had an eye to the ancient grant, in bringing them back, for that remained in force, and the discontinuance of the possession was not a defeasance of the right. He that gave it will again give it. (2.) They shall enjoy great tranquillity there. When those that have been vexatious to them are taken off they shall live in quietness; there shall be no more <hi type="italic">a pricking brier nor a grieving thorn,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.24">v. 24</reference>. They shall have a happy settlement, for they shall <hi type="italic">build houses,</hi> and <hi type="italic">plant vineyards;</hi> and they shall enjoy a happy security and serenity there; they shall <hi type="italic">dwell safely,</hi> shall <hi type="italic">dwell with confidence,</hi> and there shall be none to disquiet them or make them afraid, <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.26">v. 26</reference>. This never had full accomplishment in the body of that people, for after their return out of captivity they were ever and anon molested by some bad neighbour or other. Nor has the gospel-church been ever quite free from pricking briers and grieving thorns; yet sometimes <hi type="italic">the church has rest,</hi> and believers always dwell safely under the divine protection and may be <hi type="italic">quiet from the fear of evil.</hi> But the full accomplishment of this promise is reserved for the heavenly Canaan, when all the saints shall be gathered together, and every thing that offends shall be removed, and all griefs and fears for ever banished.  <chapter eID="Ezek.28"/> <div eID="gen18972" type="x-p"/>

entries.e69ee7074e90c48680887173d80c0b56c8b93af2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11553"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 28</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.28.1-Ezek.28.26">Eze 28:1-26</reference>. Prophetical Dirge on the King of Tyre, as the Culmination and Embodiment of the Spirit of Carnal Pride and Self-sufficiency of the Whole State. The Fall of Zidon, the Mother City. The Restoration of Israel in Contrast with Tyre and Zidon.</title> <div sID="gen20925" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11553"/><hi type="bold">2. Because, &c.--</hi>repeated resumptively in <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.6">Eze 28:6</reference>. The apodosis begins at <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.7">Eze 28:7</reference>. "The prince of Tyrus" at the time was Ithobal, or Ithbaal II; the name implying his close connection with Baal, the Phoenician supreme god, whose representative he was.<div eID="gen20925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20926" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I am a god, I sit in ... seat of God ... the seas--</hi>As God sits enthroned in His heavenly citadel exempt from all injury, so I sit secure in my impregnable stronghold amidst the stormiest elements, able to control them at will, and make them subserve my interests. The language, though primarily here applied to the king of Tyre, as similar language is to the king of Babylon (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.13">Is 14:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.14">14</reference>), yet has an ulterior and fuller accomplishment in Satan and his embodiment in Antichrist (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.25">Da 7:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.36">11:36</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.37">37</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.4">2Th 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.6">Re 13:6</reference>). This feeling of superhuman elevation in the king of Tyre was fostered by the fact that the island on which Tyre stood was called "the holy island" [Sanconiathon], being sacred to Hercules, so much so that the colonies looked up to Tyre as the mother city of their religion, as well as of their political existence. The Hebrew for "God" is El, that is, "the Mighty One."<div eID="gen20926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20927" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yet, &c.--</hi>keen irony.<div eID="gen20927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20928" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set thine heart as ... heart of God--</hi>Thou thinkest of thyself as if thou wert God. <div eID="gen20928" type="x-p"/>
entries.47b2172004451d37d8b84e7601aa1068f52646e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11554"/><div sID="gen20929" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11554"/>3. Ezekiel ironically alludes to Ithbaal's overweening opinion of the wisdom of himself and the Tyrians, as though superior to that of Daniel, whose fame had reached even Tyre as eclipsing the Chaldean sages. "Thou art wiser," namely, in thine own opinion (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.2">Zec 9:2</reference>).<div eID="gen20929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20930" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no secret--</hi>namely, forgetting riches (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.4">Eze 28:4</reference>).<div eID="gen20930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20931" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that they can hide--</hi>that is, that can be hidden. <div eID="gen20931" type="x-p"/>

Because, &c.--</hi>resumptive of <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.2">Eze 28:2</reference>. <div eID="gen20933" type="x-p"/>
entries.d71d35a99aae80340f30bc1a996ef4ba29ddceac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11557"/><div sID="gen20934" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11557"/><hi type="bold">7. therefore--</hi>apodosis.<div eID="gen20934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20935" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strangers ... terrible of the nations--</hi>the Chaldean foreigners noted for their ferocity (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.11">Eze 30:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.12">31:12</reference>).<div eID="gen20935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20936" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">against the beauty of thy wisdom--</hi>that is, against thy beautiful possessions acquired by thy wisdom on which thou pridest thyself (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.3-Ezek.28.5">Eze 28:3-5</reference>).<div eID="gen20936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20937" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">defile thy brightness--</hi>obscure the brightness of thy kingdom. <div eID="gen20937" type="x-p"/>
entries.64cef1ce76e9beec723e2d21319d7c64d90ccf42: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11558"/><div sID="gen20938" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11558"/><hi type="bold">8. the pit--</hi>that is, the bottom of the sea; the image being that of one conquered in a sea-fight.<div eID="gen20938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20939" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the deaths--</hi>plural, as various kinds of deaths are meant (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.4">Jr 16:4</reference>).<div eID="gen20939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20940" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of them ... slain--</hi>literally, "pierced through." Such deaths as those pierced with many wounds die. <div eID="gen20940" type="x-p"/>
entries.ad5b1661015305f11b37c2586c681ac9ddf512cc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11559"/><div sID="gen20941" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11559"/><hi type="bold">9. yet say--</hi>that is, still say; referring to <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.2">Eze 28:2</reference>.<div eID="gen20941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20942" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but, &c.--</hi>But thy blasphemous boastings shall be falsified, and thou shalt be shown to be but man, and not God, in the hand (at the mercy) of Him. <div eID="gen20942" type="x-p"/>
entries.f507b79f99678bef647ff35e8e9fee6ef1b9cc7f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11560"/><div sID="gen20943" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11560"/><hi type="bold">10. deaths of ... uncircumcised--</hi>that is, such a death as the uncircumcised or godless heathen deserve; and perhaps, also, such as the uncircumcised inflict, a great ignominy in the eyes of a Jew (<reference osisRef="1Sam.31.4">1Sa 31:4</reference>); a fit retribution on him who had scoffed at the circumcised Jews. <div eID="gen20943" type="x-p"/>
entries.0b1af76bcf4b71a9e2099922eabd8fc330085bd6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11561"/><div sID="gen20944" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11561"/><hi type="bold">12. sealest up the sum--</hi>literally, "Thou art the one sealing the sum of perfection." A thing is sealed when completed (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">Da 9:24</reference>). "The sum" implies the full measure of beauty, from a Hebrew root, "to measure." The normal man--one formed after accurate rule. <div eID="gen20944" type="x-p"/>
entries.d0bba052b2780b5dc9a701037f5b77632abd148b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11562"/><div sID="gen20945" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11562"/><hi type="bold">13. in Eden--</hi>The king of Tyre is represented in his former high state (contrasted with his subsequent downfall), under images drawn from the primeval man in Eden, the type of humanity in its most Godlike form.<div eID="gen20945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20946" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">garden of God--</hi>the model of ideal loveliness (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.8">Eze 31:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.35">36:35</reference>). In the person of the king of Tyre a new trial was made of humanity with the greatest earthly advantages. But as in the case of Adam, the good gifts of God were only turned into ministers to pride and self.<div eID="gen20946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20947" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every precious stone--</hi>so in Eden (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.12">Ge 2:12</reference>), "gold, bdellium, and the onyx stone." So the king of Tyre was arrayed in jewel-bespangled robes after the fashion of Oriental monarchs. The nine precious stones here mentioned answer to nine of the twelve (representing the twelve tribes) in the high priest's breastplate (<reference osisRef="Exod.39.10-Exod.39.13">Ex 39:10-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.14">Re 21:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.19-Rev.21.21">19-21</reference>). Of the four rows of three in each, the third is omitted in the Hebrew, but is supplied in the Septuagint. In this, too, there is an ulterior reference to Antichrist, who is blasphemously to arrogate the office of our divine High Priest (<reference osisRef="Zech.6.13">Zec 6:13</reference>).<div eID="gen20947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20948" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tabrets--</hi>tambourines.<div eID="gen20948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20949" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pipes--</hi>literally, "holes" in musical pipes or flutes.<div eID="gen20949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20950" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">created--</hi>that is, in the day of thine accession to the throne. Tambourines and all the marks of joy were ready prepared for thee ("in thee," that is, "with and for thee"). Thou hadst not, like others, to work thy way to the throne through arduous struggles. No sooner created than, like Adam, thou wast surrounded with the gratifications of Eden. Fairbairn, for "pipes," translates, "females" (having reference to <reference osisRef="Gen.1.27">Ge 1:27</reference>), that is, musician-women. Maurer explains the Hebrew not as to music, but as to the setting and mounting of the gems previously mentioned. <div eID="gen20950" type="x-p"/>
entries.1db5df5f675285a4e9a68a0149b31a9308da8f66: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11563"/><div sID="gen20951" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11563"/><hi type="bold">14. anointed cherub--</hi>Gesenius translates from an Aramaic root, "extended cherub." English Version, from a Hebrew root, is better. "The cherub consecrated to the Lord by the anointing oil" [Fairbairn].<div eID="gen20951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20952" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">covereth--</hi>The imagery employed by Ezekiel as a priest is from the Jewish temple, wherein the cherubim overshadowed the mercy seat, as the king of Tyre, a demi-god in his own esteem, extended his protection over the interests of Tyre. The cherub--an ideal compound of the highest kinds of animal existence and the type of redeemed man in his ultimate state of perfection--is made the image of the king of Tyre, as if the beau ideal of humanity. The pretensions of Antichrist are the ulterior reference, of whom the king of Tyre is a type. Compare "As God ... in the temple of God" (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.4">2Th 2:4</reference>).<div eID="gen20952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20953" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I have set thee--</hi>not thou set thyself (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.16">Pr 8:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.13.1">Ro 13:1</reference>).<div eID="gen20953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20954" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon the holy mountain of God--</hi>Zion, following up the image.<div eID="gen20954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20955" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in ... midst of ... stones of fire--</hi>In ambitious imagination he stood in the place of God, "under whose feet was, as it were, a pavement of sapphire," while His glory was like "devouring fire" (<reference osisRef="Exod.24.10">Ex 24:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.24.17">17</reference>). <div eID="gen20955" type="x-p"/>
entries.d5a7c684e0cbd25c5822f19f20e1b7b8757cf130: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11564"/><div sID="gen20956" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11564"/><hi type="bold">15. perfect--</hi>prosperous [Grotius], and having no defect. So Hiram was a sample of the Tyrian monarch in his early days of wisdom and prosperity (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.7">1Ki 5:7</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen20956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20957" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">till iniquity ... in thee--</hi>Like the primeval man thou hast fallen by abusing God's gifts, and so hast provoked God's wrath. <div eID="gen20957" type="x-p"/>
entries.c566b57472f2e7941111a480ec61d5afdcd48e95: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11565"/><div sID="gen20958" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11565"/><hi type="bold">16. filled the midst of thee--</hi>that is, they have filled the midst of the city; he as the head of the state being involved in the guilt of the state, which he did not check, but fostered.<div eID="gen20958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20959" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cast thee as profane--</hi>no longer treated as sacred, but driven out of the place of sanctity (see <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.14">Eze 28:14</reference>) which thou hast occupied (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.89.39">Psa 89:39</reference>). <div eID="gen20959" type="x-p"/>
entries.ce9070509ba9a2b0b42c2fc3cc7c7b40b3e420e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11566"/><div sID="gen20960" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11566"/><hi type="bold">17. brightness--</hi>thy splendor.<div eID="gen20960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20961" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lay thee before kings--</hi>as an example of God's wrath against presumptuous pride. <div eID="gen20961" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e66ef25fae6458443643681bbaf09f97c0f1e48: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11567"/><div sID="gen20962" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11567"/><hi type="bold">18. thy sanctuaries--</hi>that is, the holy places, attributed to the king of Tyre in <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.14">Eze 28:14</reference>, as his ideal position. As he "profaned" it, so God will "profane" him (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.16">Eze 28:16</reference>).<div eID="gen20962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20963" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fire ... devour--</hi>As he abused his supposed elevation amidst "the stones of fire" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.16">Eze 28:16</reference>), so God will make His "fire" to "devour" him. <div eID="gen20963" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a5167cda8c6e44c6f1f1f020ea533c54109b5f0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11568"/><div sID="gen20964" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11568"/><hi type="bold">21. Zidon--</hi>famous for its fishery (from a root, Zud, "to fish"); and afterwards for its wide extended commerce; its artistic elegance was proverbial. Founded by Canaan's first-born (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.15">Ge 10:15</reference>). Tyre was an offshoot from it, so that it was involved in the same overthrow by the Chaldeans as Tyre. It is mentioned separately, because its idolatry (Ashtaroth, Tammuz, or Adonis) infected Israel more than that of Tyre did (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.14">Eze 8:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.10.6">Jud 10:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.33">1Ki 11:33</reference>). The notorious Jezebel was a daughter of the Zidonian king. <div eID="gen20964" type="x-p"/>
entries.efe04341a63305e3a8f82b9155a812ef57f490d5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11569"/><div sID="gen20965" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11569"/><hi type="bold">22. shall be sanctified in her--</hi>when all nations shall see that I am the Holy Judge in the vengeance that I will inflict on her for sin. <div eID="gen20965" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d459dfe38134510d936bb3d531cec535c54f9ea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11570"/><div sID="gen20966" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11570"/><hi type="bold">24. no more ... brier ... unto ... Israel--</hi>as the idolatrous nations left in Canaan (among which Zidon is expressly specified in the limits of Asher, <reference osisRef="Judg.1.31">Jud 1:31</reference>) had been (<reference osisRef="Num.33.55">Nu 33:55</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.23.13">Jos 23:13</reference>). "A brier," first ensnaring the Israelites in sin, and then being made the instrument of punishing them.<div eID="gen20966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20967" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pricking--</hi>literally, "causing bitterness." The same Hebrew is translated "fretting" (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.51">Le 13:51</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.52">52</reference>). The wicked are often called "thorns" (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.6">2Sa 23:6</reference>). <div eID="gen20967" type="x-p"/>
entries.782c61b0c5032f97988db78598e171c663776353: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11571"/><div sID="gen20968" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11571"/>25-26. Fulfilled in part at the restoration from Babylon, when Judaism, so far from being merged in heathenism, made inroads by conversions on the idolatry of surrounding nations. The full accomplishment is yet future, when Israel, under Christ, shall be the center of Christendom; of which an earnest was given in the woman from the coasts of Tyre and Sidon who sought the Saviour (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.21">Mt 15:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.26-Matt.24.28">24, 26-28</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.11.12">Is 11:12</reference>).<div eID="gen20968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20969" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dwell safely--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">Jr 23:6</reference>). <chapter eID="Ezek.28"/>

entries.b809387fa4c50736b6d8579bbf7e7d6e0df6af4a: <div eID="gen32074" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen32075" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32076" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32076" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32075" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32077" type="x-p"/> The first part of this chapter relates to a King of Tyre, probably the same who is called in the Phoenician annals Ithobalus. He seems to have been a vain man, who affected Divine honors. The prophet treats his foolish pretensions with severe irony, and predicts his doom, <reference osisRef="Eze.28.1-Eze.28.10">Eze 28:1-10</reference>. He then takes up a funeral dirge and lamentation over him, in which his former pomp and splendor are finely contrasted with his fall, in terms that seem frequently to allude to the fall of Lucifer from heaven, (Isaiah 14), <reference osisRef="Eze.28.11-Eze.28.19">Eze 28:11-19</reference>. The overthrow of Sidon, the mother city of Tyre, is next announced, <reference osisRef="Eze.28.20-Eze.28.23">Eze 28:20-23</reference>; and the chapter concludes with a promise to the Jews of deliverance from all their enemies, and particularly of their restoration from the Babylonish captivity, <reference osisRef="Eze.28.24-Eze.28.26">Eze 28:24-26</reference>.
entries.405a729c2369909260fd621cc4e847d89768939f: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen32077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32078" type="x-p"/> Say unto the prince of Tyrus - But who was this prince of Tyrus? Some think Hiram; some, Sin; some, the devil; others, Ithobaal, with whom the chronology and circumstances best agree. Origen thought the guardian angel of the city was intended. <div eID="gen32078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32079" type="x-p"/> I am a god - That is, I am absolute, independent, and accountable to none. He was a man of great pride and arrogance.
entries.7210f7ea620229bc93fe3c2a2704898ec720a481: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen32079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32080" type="x-p"/> Thou art wiser than Daniel - Daniel was at this time living, and was reputable for his great wisdom. This is said ironically. See <reference osisRef="Eze.14.14">Eze 14:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.26.1">Eze 26:1</reference>.
entries.08b8bf4e3ca3f9de1d37e1db6184d4bd22261e2b: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen32080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32081" type="x-p"/> By thy great wisdom - He attributed every thing to himself; he did not acknowledge a Divine providence. As he got all by himself, so he believed he could keep all by himself, and had no need of any foreign help.
entries.bbf34722c1e731092700ea04ef5b53094ad40ba8: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen32081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32082" type="x-p"/> I will bring strangers upon thee - The Chaldeans.
entries.42086ad1f266b56db473943553c84305c82be472: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen32082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32083" type="x-p"/> Wilt thou yet say before him that slayeth thee - Wilt thou continue thy pride and arrogance when the sword is sheathed in thee, and still imagine that thou art self-sufficient and independent?
entries.b1945988bcf8168b40655bb8ab0c6f3664971cc3: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen32083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32084" type="x-p"/> The deaths of the uncircumcised - Two deaths, temporal and eternal. Ithobaal was taken and killed by Nebuchadnezzar.
entries.f677d2130b7ea91082d3e661624800563ba9e84a: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen32084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32085" type="x-p"/> Thou sealest up - This has been translated, "Thou drawest thy own likeness." "Thou formest a portrait of thyself; and hast represented thyself the perfection of wisdom and beauty." I believe this to be the meaning of the place.
entries.db0c6cc361d9c55093b642419691178cf377ab10: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen32085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32086" type="x-p"/> Thou hast been in Eden - This also is a strong irony. Thou art like Adam, when in his innocence and excellence he was in the garden of Eden! <div eID="gen32086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32087" type="x-p"/> Every precious stone was thy covering - For a description of these stones see the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.28.17">Exo 28:17</reference>.
entries.4e532c4af475990ce961c0fff6d923077b1ea074: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen32087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32088" type="x-p"/> Thou art the anointed cherub that covereth - The irony is continued; and here he is likened to the Cherub that guarded the gates of Paradise, and kept the way of the tree of life; or to one of the cherubs whose wings, spread out, covered the mercy-seat. <div eID="gen32088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32089" type="x-p"/> Thou mast upon the holy mountain of God - The irony is still continued; and now he is compared to Hoses, and afterwards to one of the chief angels, who has walked up and down among the stones of fire; that is, thy floors have been paved with precious stones, that shone and sparkled like fire. <div eID="gen32089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32090" type="x-p"/> Lucan, describing the splendor of the apartments of Cleopatra, queen of Egypt, speaks in nearly a similar language: - <div eID="gen32090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32091" type="x-p"/> Nec summis crustata domus, sectisque nitebat <div eID="gen32091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32092" type="x-p"/> Marmoribus, stabatque sibi non segnis achates, <div eID="gen32092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32093" type="x-p"/> Purpureusque lapis, totusque effusus in aula <div eID="gen32093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32094" type="x-p"/> Calcabatur onyx; <div eID="gen32094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32095" type="x-p"/> Pharsal. lib. x. <div eID="gen32095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32096" type="x-p"/> Rich as some fane by slavish zealots reared, <div eID="gen32096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32097" type="x-p"/> For the proud banquet stood the hall prepared: <div eID="gen32097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32098" type="x-p"/> Thick golden plates the latent beams infold, <div eID="gen32098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32099" type="x-p"/> And the high roof was fretted o'er with gold. <div eID="gen32099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32100" type="x-p"/> Of solid marble all the walls were made, <div eID="gen32100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32101" type="x-p"/> And onyx e'en the meaner floor inlaid; <div eID="gen32101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32102" type="x-p"/> While porphyry and agate round the court <div eID="gen32102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32103" type="x-p"/> In massy columns rose, a proud support. <div eID="gen32103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32104" type="x-p"/> Of solid ebony each post was wrought, <div eID="gen32104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32105" type="x-p"/> From swarthy Meroe profusely brought. <div eID="gen32105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32106" type="x-p"/> With ivory was the entrance crusted o'er, <div eID="gen32106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32107" type="x-p"/> And polished tortoise hid each shining door; <div eID="gen32107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32108" type="x-p"/> While on the cloudy spots enchased was seen <div eID="gen32108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32109" type="x-p"/> The trusty emerald's never-fading green. <div eID="gen32109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32110" type="x-p"/> Within the royal beds and couches shone, <div eID="gen32110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32111" type="x-p"/> Beamy and bright with many a costly stone, <div eID="gen32111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32112" type="x-p"/> The glowing purple rich. <div eID="gen32112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32113" type="x-p"/> Rowe.
entries.bafc013c9d476e4ad03ce19c8918dfb59466884a: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen32113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32114" type="x-p"/> Thou wast perfect in thy ways - The irony seems still to be kept up. Thou hast been like the angels, like Moses, like the cherubs, like Adam, like God, till thy iniquity was found out.
entries.5f860696649176ca491952e7dcafe36ea8daf2e6: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen32114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32115" type="x-p"/> I will cast thee as profane - Thou shalt be cast down from thine eminence. <div eID="gen32115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32116" type="x-p"/> From the midst of the stones of fire - Some, supposing that stones of fire means the stars, have thought that the whole refers to the fall of Satan.
entries.3772494621a7910664f0525a075553051f53fc84: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen32116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32117" type="x-p"/> Thou hast defiled thy sanctuaries - Irony continued. As God, as the angels, as the cherubim, thou must have had thy sanctuaries; but thou hast defiled them: and as Adam, thou hast polluted thy Eden, and hast been expelled from Paradise.
entries.8c6aecb14374845ca201facb6317a57742557d7d: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen32117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32118" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt be a terror - Instead of being an object of adoration thou shalt be a subject of horror, and at last be destroyed with thy city, so that nothing but thy name shall remain. It was entirely burnt by Alexander the Great, as it had been before by Nebuchadnezzar.
entries.25ebee23fd6a1dcc243e6c7a7bfbe25c5ae041b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen32118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32119" type="x-p"/> I am against thee, O Zidon - Sidon for a long time had possessed the empire of the sea and of all Phoenicia, and Tyre was one of its colonies; but in process of time, the daughter became greater than the mother. It seems to have been an independent place at the time in which Tyre was taken; but it is likely that it was taken by the Chaldeans soon after the former.
entries.a7544259eb8e477436ecd22498e488f8adf8407c: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen32119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32120" type="x-p"/> And the wounded - חלל chalal, the soldiery. All its supports shall be taken away, and its defenders destroyed.
entries.04fc2c61460ecdb226a6de047e49bfc4a0059e65: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen32120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32121" type="x-p"/> There shall be no more a pricking brier - Nothing to excite Israel to idolatry when restored from their captivity. Perhaps there is an allusion to Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal, king of Sidon, and wife to Ahab, king of Israel, who was the greatest curse to Israel, and the universal restorer of idolatry in the land, see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.31">1Kgs 16:31</reference>. Sidon being destroyed, there would come no encourager of idolatry from that quarter.
entries.552ed2a8c4dcc214c911669790de1298265350a2: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen32121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32122" type="x-p"/> When I shall have gathered the house of Israel - In their long captivity, God had been preparing the land for them so as to make it a safe dwelling; and hence he executed judgments on all the heathen nations round about by means of the Chaldeans. Thus Tyre and Sidon were destroyed, as were the Ammonites and others who had been the inveterate enemies of the Jews. Judgment first began at his own house, then proceeded to the heathen nations; and when they were brought down, then he visited and redeemed his people. Thus God's ways are proved to be all equal; partialities and caprices belong not to him.  <chapter eID="Ezek.28"/> <div eID="gen32122" type="x-p"/>

entries.2b6b618ed8ceea9a9635713664676ee21c6b39fe: <div eID="gen15059" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Against the Prince of Tyre - Ezekiel 28:1-19</title> <div sID="gen15060" type="x-p"/> As the city of Tyre was first of all threatened with destruction (Ezekiel 26), and then her fall was confirmed by a lamentation (Ezekiel 27), so here the prince of Tyre is first of all forewarned of his approaching death (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.1-Ezek.28.10">Eze 28:1-10</reference>), and then a lamentation is composed thereon (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.11-Ezek.28.19">Eze 28:11-19</reference>). <div eID="gen15060" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Fall of the Prince of Tyre</title> <div sID="gen15061" type="x-p"/> Eze 28:1. <hi type="italic">And the word of Jehovah came to me, saying,</hi> Eze 28:2. <hi type="italic">Son of man, say to the prince of Tyre, Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Because thy heart has lifted itself up, and thou sayest, “I am a God, I sit upon a seat of Gods, in the heart of the seas,” when thou art a man and not God, and cherishest a mind like a God’s mind,</hi> Eze 28:3. <hi type="italic">Behold, thou art wiser than Daniel; nothing secret is obscure to thee;</hi> Eze 28:4. <hi type="italic">Through thy wisdom and thy understanding hast thou acquired might, and put gold and silver in thy treasuries;</hi> Eze 28:5. <hi type="italic">Through the greatness of thy wisdom hast thou increased thy might by thy trade, and thy heart has lifted itself up on account of thy might,</hi> Eze 28:6. <hi type="italic">Therefore thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Because thou cherishest a mind like a God’s mind,</hi> Eze 28:7. <hi type="italic">Therefore, behold, I will bring foreigners upon thee, violent men of the nations; they will draw their swords against the beauty of thy wisdom, and pollute thy splendour.</hi> Eze 28:8. <hi type="italic">They will cast thee down into the pit, that thou mayest die the death of the slain in the heart of the seas.</hi> Eze 28:9. <hi type="italic">Wilt thou indeed say, I am a God, in the face of him that slayeth thee, when thou art a man and not God in the hand of him that killeth thee?</hi> Eze 28:10. <hi type="italic">Thou wilt die the death of the uncircumcised at the hand of foreigners; for I have spoken it, is the saying of the Lord Jehovah.</hi> - This threat of judgment follows in general the same course as those addressed to other nations (compare especially Ezekiel 25), namely, that the sin is mentioned first (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.2-Ezek.28.5">Eze 28:2-5</reference>), and then the punishment consequent upon the sin (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.6-Ezek.28.10">Eze 28:6-10</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.12">Eze 28:12</reference> מלך is used instead of נגיד, dux. In the use of the term נגיד to designate the king, Kliefoth detects an indication of the peculiar position occupied by the prince in the commercial state of Tyre, which had been reared upon municipal foundations; inasmuch as he was not so much a monarch, comparable to the rulers of Bayblon or to the Pharaohs, as the head of the great mercantile aristocracy. This is in harmony with the use of the word נגיד for the prince of Israel, David for example, whom God chose and anointed to be the <hi type="italic">nâgīd</hi> over His people; in other words, to be the leader of the tribes, who also formed an independent commonwealth (vid., <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.14">1Sa 13:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.8">2Sa 7:8</reference>, etc.). The pride of the prince of Tyre is described in <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.2">Eze 28:2</reference> as consisting in the fact that he regarded himself as a God, and his seat in the island of Tyre as a God’s seat. He calls his seat מושׁב , not “because his capital stood out from the sea, like the palace of God from the ocean of heaven” (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.3">Psa 104:3</reference>), as Hitzig supposes; for, apart from any other ground, this does not suit the subsequent description of his seat as God’s mountain (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.16">Eze 28:16</reference>), and God’s holy mountain (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.14">Eze 28:14</reference>). The God’s seat and God’s mountain are not the palace of the king of Tyre, but Tyre as a state, and that not because of its firm position upon a rocky island, but as a holy island (ἁγία νῆσος, as Tyre is called in Sanchun. ed. Orelli, p. 36), the founding of which has been glorified by myths (vid., Movers, <hi type="italic">Phoenizier</hi>, I pp. 637ff.). The words which Ezekiel puts into the mouth of the king of Tyre may be explained, as Kliefoth has well expressed it, “from the notion lying at the foundation of all natural religions, according to which every state, as the production of its physical factors and bases personified as the native deities of house and state, is regarded as a work and sanctuary of the gods.” In Tyre especially the national and political development went hand in hand with the spread and propagation of its religion. “The Tyrian state was the production and seat of its gods. He, the prince of Tyre, presided over this divine creation and divine seat; therefore he, the prince, was himself a god, a manifestation of the deity, having its work and home in the state of Tyre.” All heathen rulers looked upon themselves in this light; so that the king of Babylon is addressed in a similar manner in <reference osisRef="Isa.14.13">Isa 14:13</reference>-14. This self-deification is shown to be a delusion in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.28.2">Eze 28:2</reference></hi>; He who is only a man makes his heart like a God’s heart, i.e., cherishes the same thought as the Gods. לב, the heart, as the seat of the thoughts and imaginations, is named instead of the disposition. <div eID="gen15061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15062" type="x-p"/> This is carried out still further in <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.3-Ezek.28.5">Eze 28:3-5</reference> by a description of the various sources from which this imagination sprang. He cherishes a God’s mind, because he attributes to himself superhuman wisdom, through which he has created the greatness, and might, and wealth of Tyre. The words, “behold, thou art wiser,” etc. (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.3">Eze 28:3</reference>), are not to be taken as a question, “art thou indeed wiser?” as they have been by the lxx, Syriac, and others; nor are they ironical, as Hävernick supposes; but they are to be taken literally, namely, inasmuch as the prince of Tyre was serious in attributing to himself supernatural and divine wisdom. Thou art, i.e., thou regardest thyself as being, wiser than Daniel. No hidden thing is obscure to thee (עמם, a later word akin to the Aramaean, “to be obscure”). The comparison with Daniel refers to the fact that Daniel surpassed all the magi and wise men of Babylon in wisdom through his ability to interpret dreams, since God gave him an insight into the nature and development of the power of the world, such as no human sagacity could have secured. The wisdom of the prince of Tyre, on the other hand, consisted in the cleverness of the children of this world, which knows how to get possession of all the good things of the earth. Through such wisdom as this had the Tyrian prince acquired power and riches. חיל, might, possessions in the broader sense; not merely riches, but the whole of the might of the commercial state of Tyre, which was founded upon riches and treasures got by trade. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.5">Eze 28:5</reference> בּרכלּתך is in apposition to בּרב הכמתך, and is introduced as explanatory. The fulness of its wisdom showed itself in its commerce and the manner in which it conducted it, whereby Tyre had become rich and powerful. It is not till we reach <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.6">Eze 28:6</reference> that we meet with the apodosis answering to 'יען גּבהּ וגו in <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.2">Eze 28:2</reference>, which has been pushed so far back by the intervening parenthetical sentences in <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.2">Eze 28:2</reference>-5. For this reason the sin of the prince of Tyre in deifying himself is briefly reiterated in the clause 'יען תּתּך וגו (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.28.6">Eze 28:6</reference></hi>, compare <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.28.2">Eze 28:2</reference></hi>), after which the announcement of the punishment is introduced with a repetition of לכן in Eze 28:7. Wild foes approaching with barbarous violence will destroy all the king’s resplendent glory, slay the king himself with the sword, and hurl him down into the pit as a godless man. The enemies are called עריצי גּוים, violent ones of the peoples - that is to say, the wild hordes composing the Chaldean army (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.11">Eze 30:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.12">Eze 31:12</reference>). They drew the sword “against the beauty (יפי, the construct state of יפי) of thy wisdom,” i.e., the beauty produced by thy wisdom, and the beautiful Tyre itself, with all that it contains (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.3-Ezek.26.4">Eze 26:3-4</reference>). יפעה, splendour; it is only here and in <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.17">Eze 28:17</reference> that we meet with it as a noun.
